source.title_on_document: We're Different, We're the Same: Creative Homogeneity Across LLMs

supplement.where: Appendices A-C at the end of this PDF (pp. 16-18). The document cites no separate or online supplement.
supplement.holds: Appendix A: exact test wording for humans and LLMs. Appendix B: originality scoring formulas for the AUT, FF, and DAT (eqs. 2-4). Appendix C: t-SNE plots of FF and DAT responses (Fig. 10). The appendices add no statistics, and the document prints no standard errors anywhere.

paper_design_summary: The authors administered three divergent-thinking tests (Alternative Uses Task, Forward Flow, and Divergent Association Task) separately to 22 LLMs through public APIs and to Prolific participants, analyzing 102 people after recruiting 114 and excluding 12 (pp. 4-5, Section 3.3). They compared output originality (GloVe semantic distance) and population-level variability (cosine distance between all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings of different respondents' responses), with statistical tests described as using 7 LLMs, one per model family. Additional analyses varied the AUT and system prompts, compared five Llama models with unrelated models, and validated the Prolific responses against prior human datasets; no people were assigned AI assistance.

studies.label: LLMs vs Prolific humans on the AUT, Forward Flow, and DAT

assignment.what_was_assigned: People were not assigned to AI assistance or randomized between AI conditions. Humans completed the creativity tests; LLMs were prompted separately with the tests, worded for machine-readable output (pp. 4-5, Section 3.3; Appendix A). The authors used safeguards against human respondents' AI use but acknowledge that the risk remains (p. 5).
assignment.quote: To study this question, we elicit creative responses from humans and a broad set of LLMs using standardized creativity tests and compare the population-level diversity of responses.

arms.name: LLMs
arms.description: 22 LLMs with public APIs, default system prompt 'You are a helpful assistant'. Statistical tests use a subset of 7, one per family: AI21 Jamba 1.5 Large, Google Gemini 1.5, Cohere Command R Plus, Meta Llama 3 70B Instruct, Mistral Large, gpt 4o, Phi 3 medium 128k Instruct (p. 5). Robustness runs vary the AUT prompt (v1-v3, Section 5.1) and the system prompt (Section 5.3). Model output, not people.

arms.name: Humans (Prolific)
arms.description: Prolific participants who completed the DAT, FF, and AUT in an online survey; 102 analyzed. No AI assistance was assigned. The authors used safeguards against undisclosed AI use but acknowledge residual risk (p. 5, Section 3.3).

participants.exclusions: 114 recruited; 12 removed on suspicion of being bots, because of unusually short response times (< 5 minutes) or failed attention checks; 102 analyzed. No one was randomized, so n_randomized is null; 114 is the number recruited. The authors corrected obvious misspellings by hand.
participants.who: Prolific workers screened for English fluency and an approval rating > 95; paid $15/hour; 19 minutes on average. Table 1: 51% female, 46% male, 3% non-binary; 53% White, 28% Black or African American, 11% Hispanic or Latino, 6% Asian, 2% other; ages 18-24 22%, 25-34 31%, 35-44 23%, 45-54 19%, 55+ 5%.
participants.quote: Of these, 12 were removed on suspicion of being bots due to unusually short response times (< 5 minutes) or failed attention checks, so the final dataset contains 102 human responses.

ai_tool.name_model: 22 LLMs via public APIs (footnote 1 links to GitHub Models): AI21-Jamba-Instruct, Cohere Command R, Cohere Command R Plus, Meta Llama 3 70B Instruct, Meta Llama 3 8B Instruct, Meta Llama 3.1 405B Instruct, Meta Llama 31 70B Instruct, Meta Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Mistral large, Mistral large 2407, Mistral Nemo, Mistral small, Google Gemini 1.5, gpt 4o, gpt 4o mini, Phi 3 medium 128k instruct, Phi 3 medium 4k instruct, Phi 3 mini 128k instruct, Phi 3 mini 4k instruct, Phi 3 small 128k instruct, Phi 3 small 8k instruct, Phi 3.5 mini instruct. Statistical tests use the 7-model subset named in the LLM arm.
ai_tool.how_used: No person was assigned AI assistance; undisclosed AI use by human respondents cannot be ruled out (p. 5). Each LLM answered the tests itself (Appendix A wording; AUT prompt v3 in Section 4, v1 and v2 in Section 5.1; four system prompts in Section 5.3), and its responses are compared with human responses.

task.description: AUT: as many creative uses as possible, up to 10, for each of book, fork, table, hammer, pants. Forward Flow: from each start word (candle, table, bear, snow, toaster), write the next word that follows from the previous one, up to 20 words (the LLM prompt asks for at least 22). DAT: 10 nouns as different from each other as possible, in less than four minutes.
task.duration: Humans took 19 minutes on average to complete the survey (p. 5).

outcomes.name: Population-level AUT variability (V_AUT): cosine distance between sentence embeddings of different respondents' AUT responses
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Each respondent's uses for one AUT object are joined into one space-separated string, with punctuation and stopwords removed, and embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2; V = 1 - cosine similarity between the strings of two different respondents for the same object (eq. 1, p. 6). Higher = more variable. Robustness variants, recorded as contrasts: AUT prompt versions v1, v2, v3, and v3 with one-word answers only (Table 5, p. 11); LLM system prompts More creative, Very creative, Not creative (Table 7, p. 13).

diversity_detail.metric: Mean of V_AUT(P): cosine distance (1 - cosine similarity) between the embedded response strings of two different members of a population for the same AUT object. Higher = more diverse, so no sign reversal is needed.
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of different members within each population (LLM-LLM pairs among the 7 models; human-human pairs among the 102 analyzed participants), for each AUT object
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Welch's t-test comparing the means of the two sets of pairwise distances, significance threshold 0.01; one-sided alternative stated as mu(V(LLM)) > mu(V(Human)); no clustering by respondent is described. Effect size = difference in means / pooled SD; test power reported.
diversity_detail.notes: Eq. 1, p. 6. Fig. 2 (p. 8) shows the distributions; Fig. 3 (p. 9) shows a t-SNE of AUT embeddings. The Llama-family comparison (Table 6) is S3.

company_involvement.description: None stated. Authors at Duke University and Technion; the only acknowledgment thanks Austin Liu for help with the system prompts; no funding statement. The models were accessed through public APIs (footnote 1 links to GitHub Models documentation).

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is not met: creativity tests were administered separately to LLMs and people, with no random assignment of people to generative-AI assistance (pp. 4-5, Section 3.3; pp. 16-17, Appendix A). Criterion 2 is met: 114 people were recruited, 12 excluded, and 102 analyzed; the LLM counts are models, not people (p. 5, Section 3.3, Human subjects). Criterion 3 is met: originality and population-level variability are computed on the test responses (p. 6, Section 3.4 and eq. 1; p. 18, Appendix B, eqs. 2-4). S2 compares human samples and S3 compares models; neither supplies an eligible AI-assistance experiment. The paper is retained as AI-versus-human context evidence.

one_line_finding: Responses from 7 LLMs of different families were far less variable across respondents than responses from the 102 Prolific participants analyzed on the AUT (mean cosine distance 0.459 vs 0.738, effect size 2.2), Forward Flow (0.534 vs 0.835, 2.0), and DAT (0.665 vs 0.819, 1.4) (p. 8, Table 3), while LLM originality was higher on the AUT and DAT and lower on Forward Flow, with effect sizes of 0.1 to 0.77 (p. 7, Table 2).
open_questions: The number of responses per LLM (one run or several per prompt), and thus the numbers of outputs and pairs behind each t-test, is not stated; only degrees of freedom are printed (pp. 5-8, 10-13).

Section 3.3 (p. 5) specifies the 7-model subset for statistical tests, supporting that coding for Table 2. The models included in the Fig. 1 originality distributions (p. 7) are not separately specified.

The reported tests use response-level originality scores and pairwise variability scores; no respondent-clustered uncertainty is described (pp. 6-7, 18). A respondent-aware reanalysis would require responses linked to their human or model source.
Section 5.2 (pp. 11-12) does not list the baseline set of otherwise unrelated models used in Table 6, so the S3 control arm remains described only as the paper names it.
S2 reports prior-study sample sizes of 141 (DAT), 92 (AUT), and 146 (FF), but no unique combined participant total or cross-dataset overlap (p. 13, Section 5.4); its total n_analyzed remains null.
notes: Reconciled from screeners A and B against the full PDF (18 pages, references and Appendices A-C included); PDF page numbers equal printed page numbers. The markdown conversion scrambles Table 7 (p. 13) and drops the equations, so every number was checked on the PDF page images. Paper-internal inconsistencies, recorded as printed: (1) p. 7 text says 'Table 1 gives statistics comparing population means', but those statistics are in Table 2 (Table 1 is demographics). (2) The human AUT originality mean is 0.696 in Tables 2 and 4 but 0.695 in Table 7. (3) The list of 22 models (pp. 4-5) names 'AI21-Jamba-Instruct', while the 7-model subset (pp. 5, 7) names 'AI21 Jamba 1.5 Large'. (4) Tables 2-5 state the alternative as mu(LLM) > mu(Human), including Table 3, where the LLM means are lower and the difference is called significant; the printed t statistics are negative when the LLM mean is higher. (5) The Table 6 caption says the Llama models have 'lower population-level creativity', while t(248) = 0.2, p = 0.41 and the text says the difference is not statistically significant. (6) Section 5.4 opens by saying the Prolific respondents show 'equal or greater population-level variability' on the AUT and FF, but Fig. 9 reports lower variability on the AUT (prior study higher, t(1046) = 11.0); the text gives p < 0.0001 for FF and DAT where the Fig. 9 caption gives p < 0.001; and the text says prior studies score higher 'at a significant level of p <= 0.001' where the Fig. 8 caption says the AUT and DAT differences are significant 'at the 0.01 level but not the 0.001 level'. (7) Table 5 prints the same t(10078) for the one-word row as for the full v3 row, and Table 7 prints t(10078) for all four system prompts. (8) Humans write up to 20 Forward Flow words, while the LLM prompt asks for 'at least 22 words' (p. 17). Coding choices: the LLM arm counts models, not people (22 tested, 7 in the tests), so its n is null; arms[].ai is generative_ai for the LLM output arm, though no person was assigned AI assistance. The paper's effect size is the mean difference over the pooled SD of output-level or pair-level scores, not a participant-level standardized effect. The AUT used 5 objects in Sections 4, 5.1, and 5.3 and 10 objects in Section 5.2 (p. 12; Appendix A.1). S3 (model-only) is kept with its Table 6 outcome because the source prints it; its question is 'none' and its design is model_only, so it enters no pooled estimate. Finalization (2026-10-08): read the complete markdown, including references and Appendices A-C, and reconfirmed participant counts, methods, all recorded table statistics, and Fig. 8-9 caption statistics using PyMuPDF page text. No challenge files matched forms/challenges/c024.*.json; the final challenge counters are therefore zero. All reconciliation differences were already marked resolved, and the reconciliation object is preserved unchanged. Final edits identify post-exclusion counts as analyzed and distinguish no assigned AI assistance from the authors' acknowledged risk of undisclosed AI use. The Table 2 model-subset question is settled by Section 3.3 for statistical tests; the remaining Fig. 1 membership question is retained. S2 remains design_class other: it compares human datasets for validation and does not reanalyze an AI-assistance experiment or an original randomized treatment contrast (pp. 5, 13-14). All final eligibility judgments refer to the saved arXiv v1 PDF identified in source.version.

differences.a: Adds 'p_value_only' to every contrast that prints a t statistic, and 'figure_only' to the Fig. 8 and Fig. 9 caption contrasts.

Tables 2-6 print an effect size defined as the mean difference over the pooled SD (standardized_effect); Table 7 and the figure captions print none. Word overlap (Fig. 4) stays figure_only.
differences.quote: For context, we also report the effect size, which is the difference between the means of the two populations divided by their pooled standard deviation.

differences.field: studies[S2].outcomes (number of outcomes; construct, measure, unit, diversity_detail)
differences.a: Two outcomes: S2-O1 individual originality (novelty, automated_score, unit output); S2-O2 population-level variability (diversity, embedding_similarity, unit pair, diversity_detail filled).
differences.b: One combined outcome: construct 'other', measure automated_score, unit output, diversity_detail empty.
differences.resolved: A's two outcomes. The paper runs two separate comparisons with different measures and tests: originality scores (Fig. 8, one-sided t-tests) and pairwise embedding distances (Fig. 9, two-sided t-tests). Originality is novelty scored by automated_score on each output; variability is diversity scored by embedding_similarity on pairs.
differences.quote: We test both the individual originality of our human responses and population-level variability and find that while respondents in prior studies score better individually on the tests, respondents to our study exhibit equal or greater population-level variability
differences.locator: p. 13, Section 5.4 and Fig. 8; p. 14, Fig. 9

differences.a: Treatment = our study (Prolific), control = prior studies; originality treatment_lower; variability mixed.
differences.b: Treatment = prior studies, control = this study; one contrast, direction mixed.
differences.resolved: A's orientation: the paper checks its own Prolific sample against the prior datasets as the reference, so the Prolific sample is the treatment arm. Originality: treatment_lower (prior studies higher on all three tests). Variability: mixed (prior higher on the AUT; this study higher on FF and DAT).
differences.quote: Humans in prior studies have higher individual originality scores than humans in our study for all three tests. [...] Our study responses have higher population-level variability than the prior study on the DAT and FF tests

open_items.item: LLM repeat counts and numbers of outputs/pairs per test are unstated (pp. 5-8, 10-13). Authors' generation logs and analysis inputs would establish these counts. They concern model/output units and do not alter the 102 analyzed people or the absence of random assignment to AI assistance.

Table 2/Fig. 1 model subset: Section 3.3 (p. 5) specifies the 7-model subset for statistical tests, settling the Table 2 coding. Fig. 1 (p. 7) does not separately identify its plotted models; the authors' plotting inputs would settle that remaining part. Plot membership affects no eligibility criterion.

Participant/model dependence in uncertainty: the paper reports tests on response-level or pairwise scores without respondent-clustered uncertainty (pp. 6-7, 18). Posted responses with respondent/model identifiers would permit a reanalysis accounting for this dependence. This concerns precision, not any of the three eligibility criteria.

S3 baseline model identities are not listed in Section 5.2 (pp. 11-12). The authors' model roster for Table 6 would settle this. S3 has no human participants, so these identities cannot make it eligible.

S2 prior-study counts are reported separately by test (141 DAT, 92 AUT, 146 FF; p. 13, Section 5.4); a unique combined total is unstated and remains null. Participant identifiers or overlap documentation in the posted datasets would settle the combined count. S1 already has 102 analyzed people, and S2 has no AI-assistance assignment, so eligibility is unaffected.
